toc.title: A pitfall: talking about what led you to freeze
A light practice: skipping a stone

blocks.p: There's a really good chance you exist in a freeze state. Let's walk through what freeze is through the Polyvagal Theory, a couple of pitfalls in addressing it, and what you can do to start coming out of it.

Freeze is a combination of the sympathetic flight or fight state plus the dorsal vagal shutdown state of immobilization. If you can't be safe, and you can't run away from or fight a danger, you'll go into shutdown. Freeze is shutdown and flight or fight together.

So that's being mobilized and immobilized at the same time. You could be immobilized through force, or immobilized through perception. Basically, the accelerator and the brake are on at the same time. The body is highly revved up. Heart rate is up. Muscles are tense. It's ready to move, but it can't.
If that sounds like a panic attack, that pretty much wraps it up nicely.
Freeze can have a couple of different feels to it, or flavors, as I often call them. It's the immobilization of shutdown plus flight or fight, but really it's flight or fight.

ul: Flight-flavored freeze: when you're immobilized while in flight, it feels more like panic and intense chronic anxiety.

Fight-flavored freeze: when you're immobilized while in fight, you'll have more underlying chronic anger, control issues, bullying, abuse, that kind of stuff. That underlying rage, and explosive rage, really comes from fight-flavored freeze.

blocks.p: The most important thing to know is that freeze is a combination of sympathetic flight or fight plus dorsal vagal shutdown. Revved up, but the brake is also on.

blocks.h: A pitfall: talking about what led you to freeze

blocks.p: Freeze is really difficult to work through. It's not a quick process. The problem I see in how we address freeze is that we tend to talk about the context that led to it. That's not a bad thing in and of itself. But if you start talking about the traumatic incidents that led you to freeze, it might just end up reinforcing the freeze.

Talking about stuff isn't necessarily helpful. It might actually be downright reinforcing of the state you're in. So if you have a therapist who is pushing you to talk about what you've been through, the trauma narrative, that could be reinforcing your freeze.

To come out of freeze, just like the other defensive states, you need a nice strong anchoring in your safety state. Your safety state has to be strong enough to allow the immobilization of freeze to come off, and then, eventually, to release the flight or fight activation.

In polyvagal terms, this is the vagal brake: the influence of your safety state on your heart. The vagal brake has to be strengthened enough to allow self-regulation. It has to be strong enough for the immobilization to come off, and then for the flight or fight activation to be used or discharged through some means. That's different for everybody.
So when you talk about the trauma narrative, the things you went through, and your vagal brake or your safety state isn't strong enough yet, it just ends up reinforcing your stuck defensive state.

You'll know your safety state is strong enough if you're genuinely curious and interested in all of you. If you're genuinely curious about what it feels like to be you, what it feels like to have your freeze stuck inside of you, and you're open to what comes of it when you pay attention to it.

If that sounds terrifying, that's probably a pretty good indication you're not quite there yet. And that's totally okay. It just tells us we need to work on the safety state more. As you access and build the strength of your safety state, the freeze can thaw and the flight or fight can discharge.

Here's the image I use with my therapy and coaching clients. I put my fist out and say, "This is the flight or fight activation." By itself, it's active. It's vibrating. It's ready to roll, ready to run away, ready to fight.
Then I put my other hand over the fist and say, "This is the shutdown immobilization that is freezing the flight or fight activation in place." It's locking it in.

To come out of freeze, the hand has to come off. The immobilization has to unlock, to slowly melt away, so the freeze can thaw. As it melts away, that opens up the capacity for the flight or fight activation to discharge, to be used.
That doesn't happen all at once. It's a slow process, and I think it should be. We don't want a big, out-of-control, chaotic, panicky, rageful, or overwhelming blowup. We want it to be under control.
The safety state has to be able to maintain the thaw of freeze. So the order is: get the safety state active, let the freeze come off, and then use the flight or fight activation.

An unrealistic expectation I see is that we'll go into a therapy session, do the whole shaking and trembling, release our trauma, and be good to go. That's not the way it works. I've had sessions where there's the shaking and the trembling and the release. It can be a really good sign: the person was mindful enough to really feel and release some of what was happening within them, and to get to the next step. But it doesn't mean the problem is solved. It's not the final answer in trauma recovery. It's a long process.

Coming out of freeze can be a very overwhelming experience, especially if it's new. You start touching on this stuff, and the body says, "Cool, let's self-regulate!" and it wants everything to come up all at once.
Irene Lyon described this well on the podcast:

q: The moment the safety comes up, what does it allow the system to do? It allows it to express all the stored stuff that has been in there forever.

blocks.p: That's exactly why we go slowly.

blocks.h: A light practice: skipping a stone

blocks.p: The safety state is always the priority. Here's the practice, in order:

ol: Practice safety in micro moments. Every day, in micro moments, not thirty-minute meditations. Use your senses. Mindfully experience what it feels like to be safe in your body. Notice where safety lives in your body.

Wait for curiosity. As that gets easier and you have the capacity for more safety, you can start to be curious about the flight or fight activation within you, or notice when that curiosity shows up on its own.
Touch the defense very briefly. Feel safety, touch on the flight or fight activation within you, just very briefly, and come back to safety.
Go back and forth a few times. That back and forth is called pendulation. Do it just a few times, until it feels like enough. Then move on with your day, and do the same thing the next day.

blocks.p: Do it like you're skipping a stone across the water: touch on safety, touch on the defense, touch on safety. Just real quick. Over time, hopefully, you notice that safety builds and the flight or fight activation becomes more tolerable. And over time, some more permanent unstucking can happen. We're talking about super easy, light practices here.

I had a session with someone who had done a lot of therapy before me, a lot of Somatic Experiencing work. This person would go all in: "I'm going to do all these things at once. I'm going to feel all my shutdown all at once." They kind of knew intuitively what to do, and they'd had a lot of guided practice, which was nice. But there was a lot of freeze underlying that motivation to go all in.

So instead, because going all in might actually be reinforcing all of it, I recommended we lightly touch on these things. Instead of closing your eyes and immersing yourself in safety for some thirty-minute meditation, just lightly touch on it, notice what it feels like, and keep moving on with your day. It doesn't have to be an all-in thing.

So if you notice a lot of freeze within you, that panicky, rageful stuff underlying and flavoring your existence, touch on safety first and build it up. Then touch on the defensive activation lightly.

Once you get deep enough into safety, you can notice where the defensive activation lives in your body. You can mindfully experience it. You can use description. That's a whole separate process, but it's way down the road. If you're just starting out with these practices, lightly touch on these things.

You don't have to go into the trauma narrative. You don't have to think about past stuff. It might come up, but if I were you, I'd really focus on feeling safety in the present moment, in micro moments.

So, now: can you mindfully experience the taste of a strawberry? Can you mindfully look your pet in the eyes, smile, and pet them? Can you mindfully take a walk outside and feel the sunshine or the breeze on your skin, or smell the flowers? Can you mindfully give your spouse a hug?
Micro moments of mindfulness, micro moments of safety and connection. Then, over time, micro moments of lightly touching on defense, and back to safety.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.
